Ethernet and Wi-Fi need compatible local-link specifications, which IEEE develops. Internet protocols need rules that work across interconnected networks, which IETF develops.
Match the organization to the scope: local-link technologies versus Internet protocols.
A router reads IP information to choose the next network hop. A local Ethernet frame uses MAC addresses for the current link, so these are separate responsibilities.
Across networks points to Network; across one local link points to Data Link.
The physical job makes bits measurable as voltage, light or radio. The transport job uses endpoints such as ports to deliver data to the right application process.
Signals cross the medium; transport connects the programs.
A receiver must interpret a data format, which is the Presentation responsibility. Coordinating the beginning, continuation and end of a conversation is the Session responsibility.
How it is represented versus how the conversation is managed.
OSI separates Application, Presentation and Session. The five-layer course model groups those three jobs into Application, reducing the count by two: seven becomes five.
The difference is grouping jobs, not deleting the need for those jobs.
A program can keep using the same interface to a lower layer even if that layer's implementation changes. Clear job boundaries reduce the effects of a change.
Separate jobs make faults easier to isolate and changes easier to contain.
A receiver needs a detectable physical change. Copper interfaces detect electrical changes; optical receivers detect light arriving through fiber.
The medium determines which physical signal can travel along it.
Twisting the two conductors helps reduce unwanted interference and coupling between nearby pairs. Unshielded means a metallic shield is absent.
The twist is a useful construction feature, not a routing or transport protocol.
Multiple modes can arrive at different times and spread a light pulse. Single-mode avoids that multiple-mode spreading, making longer links possible with suitable optics.
Core size and optics affect reach; neither fiber type has one universal distance.
A carrier can encode information by varying its height, repetition rate or relative cycle position. Those are amplitude, frequency and phase respectively.
AM: height. FM: repeats per second. PM: position relative to a reference.
Separate frequency bands allow simultaneous streams. Separate time slots allow streams to take turns on the same resource.
FDM separates where in frequency; TDM separates when.
At a suitable angle, light in the higher-index core reflects at the lower-index cladding boundary, helping guide the signal along the fiber.
The optical boundary and angle keep the light guided; it is not IP routing inside the cable.
A receiver checks the FCS against a newly computed value to detect corruption. Payload names the contents being carried, which may be an entire IP packet.
FCS checks the wrapper and contents; payload is what that wrapper carries.
Three bytes form the 24-bit organization prefix. The other three bytes provide values assigned within that prefix; locally assigned addresses need not identify a manufacturer.
Count the byte pairs: three plus three gives six bytes, or 48 bits.
If two senders chose the same retry time, they could collide again immediately. Randomized delays reduce repeated simultaneous attempts.
Different waiting times help break a tie on shared half-duplex Ethernet.
Eight bits are grouped as one byte. Four bits have 2⁴ = 16 patterns, exactly matching the sixteen hex digit values, so two hex digits represent a byte.
One hex digit is four bits; two hex digits are eight bits.
Independent links meeting at a central device form a star. A single common path shared by devices forms a bus.
Trace the links: spokes to a center or stops along one shared line.
The slash prefix counts network positions. IPv4 has 32 positions altogether, so taking 17 leaves 32 − 17 = 15 for the host portion.
These blanks ask for bits, not 2¹⁵ address combinations.
IPv4 has four octets of eight bits each: 4 × 8 = 32. IPv6 has eight groups of sixteen bits: 8 × 16 = 128.
A shortened IPv6 spelling still represents a full 128-bit address.
All-zero host bits select the start of the ordinary subnet; all-one host bits select its end. Those two values are reserved instead of being assigned to individual interfaces.
Zero for the network, ones for broadcast; /31 point-to-point and /32 are exceptions.
Ping times echo requests and replies. Traceroute sends probes with increasing hop limits so progressively later routers may identify themselves when the limit expires.
A silent probe response does not by itself prove a router or host is down.
A campus needs device attachment, aggregation and policy, and a reliable inter-region backbone. Access, Distribution and Core name these three design roles.
These are campus equipment roles in Chapter 12, not the OSI communication layers.
An address plan and intended connectivity can be specified before choosing equipment. Physical design selects installable devices and media to realize that logical plan.
Organization first; hardware and placement implement it.
Work-area cable runs terminate in a local telecommunications room. Backbone runs then interconnect distribution spaces rather than running to every desk.
Room to desk is horizontal; distribution space to distribution space is backbone.
A manager needs a program on the remote device to answer requests: the agent. It also needs agreed definitions to interpret those values: the MIB's managed objects.
Agent supplies the reading; MIB defines what the reading means.
